newsitem.title: UK: Peru leader keeps hard line ahead of hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru leader keeps hard line ahead of hostage talks.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, speaking in London just before the resumption in Lima on Tuesday of negotiations to end the hostage crisis in his capital, maintained his hard line of refusing to pay ransom or free rebel prisoners.

But he insisted he was optimistic that there would be a peaceful settlement and held out hope for asylum for the rebels who have been holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for almost two months.
"Definitely the Peruvian government is not going to pay any ransom," he told a packed new conference in London where he is on an official visit.
He also cautioned against Japanese companies contemplating paying out money themselves to secure the release of employees being held hostage.
"I strongly recommend that they do not pay. This would be very bad for Japanese businessmen's security in the future."

A member of the Marxist MRTA rebel group and a Peruvian government negotiator are due to meet later in the day in Lima to try to end the siege which began on December 17 when heavily armed rebels seized 500 guests at a cocktail party.

These are preliminary talks ahead of possible negotiations with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini who is demanding the release of members of his group from Peruvian jails in return for ending the siege, Fujimori said.
He dismissed any chance of releasing MRTA prisoners, saying it would simply create a danger for the thousands of tourists who visit Peru.
The expected amnesty for up to 200 prisoners later this month would not include any rebels.
"If they are innocent, they are not members of MRTA," he added.
He also doubted that the rebels would be prepared to accept safe passage to hide out in the jungle, unless MRTA prisoners were set free.
The government is looking at the possibility of asylum but has had no success so far.
Fujimori denied, after repeated questions, that he was going to Romania or anywhere else in Eastern Europe, which have been rumoured as possible countries for the rebels to take refuge.
"I fly direct to Lima (from London) with two stopovers," he said. He did not name the stopovers.
But, he suggested that Cuba might be asked to help.
"I have not yet had any contact with Cuba. (President) Fidel Castro is a personal friend ...if necessary I'll make a call to Fidel Castro. Why not?" he said.
There were no plans to bring any international or regional organisation in to mediate with the rebels which he labelled too insignificant to warrant such intervention.
"This problem won't affect the investment, trade and economy in general because it is an isolated case."
He warned there was no much room left for negotiations but hoped for a peaceful end to the crisis.
"Don't be pessimistic. We always have to work with optimism."
